abstract: Affective significance often enhances episodic memory, with stronger effects on recollection than on familiarity, but prior research has focused primarily on within-person manipulations of emotional valence. Here, we tested a novel question: whether stable individual differences in the personal significance of food were associated with long-term memory across individuals, given that food ranges from highly appetitive to strongly avoided. Across two experiments, we examined familiarity-based memory (using an image recognition task) and recollection-based memory (using a spatial source recognition task) for food and nonfood stimuli as a function of eating-related individual differences in young adults. In Experiment 1, familiarity-based recognition memory was largely unrelated to eating behavior. In Experiment 2, however, greater restrictive eating and fear of negative consequences from eating were associated with poorer recollection-based memory for food when compared to nonfood stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in the affective significance of food do not correlate with episodic memory uniformly but instead are selectively associated with reduced recollection, but not familiarity, of food relative to neutral stimuli.
